What these numbers mean

What each value measures, why it changes, and how to read it.

Distance from Earth
The straight-line distance between the spacecraft and Earth, calculated from both positions. Because Earth circles the Sun, this number swings by up to about ±0.8 AU over a year — for a few months each year it even shrinks, while Earth moves toward the probe faster than the probe moves away.
Distance from the Sun
The steadier number: it only ever grows. This is the figure scientists use when they talk about the heliosphere and interstellar space.
One-way light time
How long a radio signal, travelling at the speed of light, needs to cover the Earth distance. A command and its reply take twice as long, which is why the mission team plans every action days in advance.
Speed
Speed relative to the Sun. No engine is pushing: both probes coast on momentum gained at launch and from planetary gravity assists, and the Sun’s pull slows them by only a few metres per second each year. The second line shows how fast the Earth distance is changing today, which includes Earth’s own orbital motion.
Scale
Neptune, the outermost planet, orbits about 30 AU from the Sun. Comparing with it gives a feel for how far beyond the planets the Voyagers now are.
Where the numbers come from
Your browser propagates a NASA/JPL Horizons state vector forward in time about ten times per second. Checked against JPL’s own predictions, the Earth distance agrees to within a few tens of thousands of kilometres — but it is still an estimate, not a measurement received from the spacecraft.

Independent project: figures are calculated estimates, not official NASA telemetry. The model, its validation and its limits are explained on How It Works.

Why Voyager Tracker?

Voyager Tracker is an independent educational website about NASA’s Voyager 1 and Voyager 2. Its core is a small calculation engine: it takes the position and velocity that NASA/JPL’s Horizons system publishes for each probe and moves them forward in time, together with Earth’s position on its orbit, to estimate where the Voyagers are at this moment.

Around that engine, the site explains the mission in its own words: what each spacecraft did, what scientists learned, why the two probes differ and why the distance from Earth sometimes shrinks. It does not represent NASA or JPL, and it never presents its estimates as official telemetry.

Official data vs. this site’s estimates

Official sourceCalculatedHypotheticalEducational

  • Current distance, speed and light time: calculated here, labelled “estimate”, validated against JPL predictions.
  • Travel-time comparisons in the calculators: hypothetical illustrations only.

Two spacecraft, two different journeys

Voyager 1

Launched 5 September 1977

Took the faster route: Jupiter in 1979, Saturn and its moon Titan in 1980. The Titan flyby flung it north out of the planets’ plane, ending its planetary tour but setting it on the quickest path out of the solar system. In 1990 it took the “Pale Blue Dot” image of Earth, and in 2012 it became the first human-made object in interstellar space.

Voyager 1 in detail

Voyager 2

Launched 20 August 1977

Launched first but on a slower path that let it keep going: Jupiter (1979), Saturn (1981), Uranus (1986) and Neptune (1989). It is still the only spacecraft to have visited the two outermost planets. It crossed into interstellar space in 2018, heading south of the planets’ plane.

Voyager 2 in detail
